A missing value is information that was never collected, and an estimate
computed from incomplete data is less precise than the same estimate from
complete data would have been. How much less depends on the estimate, not on
the share of values that are missing: a parameter estimated mostly from fully
observed variables loses little, and one that rests on the incomplete
variables can lose most of what complete data would have given it. An
analysis of incomplete data has five questions to answer, and the functions
below answer them.

1. **What is missing?** The patterns of observed and missing values, and the
   number of cases behind each variance and covariance, are the description a
   reader needs before any model is fit.
2. **Which estimators stay consistent?** Listwise deletion is consistent only
   when values are missing completely at random. Full information maximum
   likelihood (FIML), two-stage maximum likelihood, and multiple imputation
   are consistent when values are missing at random given the variables in
   the analysis.
3. **What did the missing values cost?** The fraction of missing information
   of a parameter is the share of its sampling variance that is due to the
   missing values. In the terms of accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE),
   it gives the number of complete cases the incomplete data were worth, the
   number of incomplete cases that would make up the loss, and how much wider
   each confidence interval is than complete data would have made it.
4. **What changes in a small sample?** A Wald interval refers its estimate to
   the normal distribution, and when the effective sample size is small a
   *t* reference distribution is the better approximation.
5. **What follows for measurement and for the next study?** Reliability
   coefficients, factor scores, and sample size plans each carry the missing
   information forward.

| Function | What it reports |
|:--|:--|
| `missing_patterns()` | The distinct patterns of observed and missing items, with their counts |
| `missing_coverage()` | The number and proportion of cases that observed each pair of items |
| `fa_confirmatory()` | A confirmatory factor model fitted by full information maximum likelihood, its default |
| `fraction_missing_information()` | The fraction of missing information of every parameter, with the effective sample size, the target sample size, and the width inflation factor |
| `cov_fiml()` | The maximum likelihood (EM) covariance matrix and means of incomplete items |
| `df_missing()`, `wald_df` | Degrees of freedom for a *t* reference distribution from each parameter's fraction of missing information |
| `df_barnard_rubin()` | Degrees of freedom for an estimate pooled over multiple imputations |
| `fa_confirmatory(..., missing = "two_stage")` | Two-stage maximum likelihood, with its residual based test statistic and corrected fit indices |
| `reliability_omega()`, `reliability_alpha()`, `reliability_omega_categorical()` | Reliability coefficients from incomplete items, with their intervals |
| `factor_scores()` | Factor scores with standard errors, intervals, and determinacy for each missing data pattern |
| `ss_aipe_reliability(..., fmi = )`, `ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()` | A sample size plan for a reliability interval that will be estimated from incomplete data, and its check by simulation |

The models are fitted with lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), which must be installed to
run the code below; the two sections that impute also use mice (van Buuren &
Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).

## The Running Example

Holzinger and Swineford (1939) gave ability tests to the seventh and eighth
grade pupils of two Chicago schools, and `holzinger_swineford` holds the
scores of all 301 pupils. Four of the tests measured
spatial ability: visual perception, cubes, paper form board, and lozenges.
Two more, a revised paper form board and a flags test, were tried at the
Grant-White school as experimental substitutes for the paper form board and
lozenges tests and were never given at Pasteur. The six spatial tests are the
running example.


``` r
library(DMAR)
spatial <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t3_paper_form_board",
             "t4_lozenges", "t25_paper_form_board_r", "t26_flags")
d <- descriptives(holzinger_swineford[spatial])$descriptives
print(d[, c("variable", "n", "n_missing", "mean", "sd")], digits = 3)
#>                 variable   n n_missing mean   sd
#> 1   t1_visual_perception 301         0 29.6 7.00
#> 2               t2_cubes 301         0 24.4 4.71
#> 3    t3_paper_form_board 301         0 14.2 2.83
#> 4            t4_lozenges 301         0 18.0 9.05
#> 5 t25_paper_form_board_r 145       156 15.6 3.09
#> 6              t26_flags 145       156 36.3 8.34
table(holzinger_swineford$school)
#> 
#> Grant-White     Pasteur 
#>         145         156
```



The revised paper form board and the flags test are missing for all
156 Pasteur pupils and observed for all 145 Grant-White pupils. The
reason each value is missing is known, and it was a decision of the
investigators rather than of the pupils, which makes these data a clear case
to learn from. It is also a real one: the two schools differ, and the
difference will matter.

## Look Before Fitting

The first description of incomplete data is the set of patterns in which the
values are missing.


``` r
pat <- missing_patterns(holzinger_swineford, items = spatial)
pat
```



|pattern |missing_items                     |n   |proportion |n_observed |n_missing |
|:-------|:---------------------------------|:---|:----------|:----------|:---------|
|111100  |t25_paper_form_board_r, t26_flags |156 |0.518      |4          |2         |
|111111  |                                  |145 |0.482      |6          |0         |



A pattern is a string of 1s (observed) and 0s (missing), one character per
test in the order of `spatial`. There are 2
patterns, and the complete one holds the 145 pupils
that listwise deletion would keep, 48.2
percent of the sample. A FIML analysis uses every pupil with at least one
observed test, here all 301. A case missing every item would be listed
as its own pattern, since lavaan sets such cases aside without reporting
them.

The second description is the number of cases behind each covariance.


``` r
cov_pairs <- missing_coverage(holzinger_swineford, items = spatial)
cov_pairs[cov_pairs$coverage < 1, ]
```



|var_1                  |var_2                  |n_both |coverage |
|:----------------------|:----------------------|:------|:--------|
|t1_visual_perception   |t25_paper_form_board_r |145    |0.482    |
|t1_visual_perception   |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |
|t2_cubes               |t25_paper_form_board_r |145    |0.482    |
|t2_cubes               |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |
|t3_paper_form_board    |t25_paper_form_board_r |145    |0.482    |
|t3_paper_form_board    |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |
|t4_lozenges            |t25_paper_form_board_r |145    |0.482    |
|t4_lozenges            |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |
|t25_paper_form_board_r |t25_paper_form_board_r |145    |0.482    |
|t25_paper_form_board_r |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |
|t26_flags              |t26_flags              |145    |0.482    |



Every pair that involves the revised paper form board or the flags test was
observed together by the same 145 pupils. Coverage
matters for two reasons. A covariance whose two variables were never observed
together is not estimable from the data at all, and `cov_fiml()` refuses such
a pair by name; planned missing designs are built so that no pair is empty.
And when values are missing completely at random, the fraction of missing
information of any parameter is bounded by the largest univariate and
pairwise rates of missing values (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012, p. 490), here
0.518. Whether these values are missing
completely at random is the next question.

## Fitting by Full Information Maximum Likelihood

### What Each Estimator Assumes

Rubin (1976) distinguished three mechanisms. Values are missing completely at
random (MCAR) when whether a value is missing is unrelated to anything in the
data, observed or not. They are missing at random (MAR) when it may depend on
values that were observed but, given those, not on the values that are
missing. They are missing not at random (MNAR) when it depends on the missing
values themselves. The three are statements about the variables in a given
analysis, so a mechanism that is MNAR for one set of variables can be MAR for
a larger set that includes the cause of the missingness.

Listwise deletion analyzes the complete cases as if they were a random sample
from the population, which they are under MCAR. When the values are not
MCAR, the complete cases can be unrepresentative and its estimates biased;
case deletion is generally valid only under MCAR (Schafer & Graham, 2002,
p. 155). Even under MCAR it discards the observed values of every incomplete
case. FIML maximizes the likelihood of each case's observed values. Under MAR,
and when the parameters of the process that produced the missing values are
distinct from those of the model, that process can be ignored in likelihood
inference (Rubin, 1976), so FIML is consistent and efficient under MAR given
the variables in the model, provided the model for those variables is right
(Enders, 2010; Schafer & Graham, 2002). MAR cannot in general be tested
from the data at hand (Schafer & Graham, 2002, p. 152), and no estimator
discussed here protects against MNAR.

### The Planned Missingness in These Data

Listwise deletion of the six spatial tests analyzes the Grant-White pupils
alone. For the four tests every pupil took, that is visibly a different
population: the Pasteur pupils averaged
19.90 on lozenges and the Grant-White
pupils 15.97. The single-factor
model, with each factor's variance fixed at 1 so that every loading is
estimated, is fitted both ways. FIML, the default of `fa_confirmatory()`
(written out here), makes the item means part of the model; the listwise fit
is asked for with `missing = "listwise"`, and for the means with
`meanstructure = TRUE`.


``` r
spatial_factor <- list(spatial = spatial)
fit_sp  <- fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
                 missing = "fiml", output = "fit")
tab_sp  <- fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
                 missing = "fiml")
tab_lw  <- fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
                 missing = "listwise", meanstructure = TRUE)

# Estimate and 95% confidence interval of named rows, for display.
est_ci <- function(tab, terms) {
  i <- match(terms, tab$term)
  sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", tab$estimate[i], tab$ci_lower[i],
          tab$ci_upper[i])
}
means <- paste0("nu_spatial_", 1:6)
# all_pupils is NA for the two tests no Pasteur pupil took.
data.frame(test = spatial, all_pupils = colMeans(holzinger_swineford[spatial]),
           fiml = est_ci(tab_sp, means), listwise = est_ci(tab_lw, means),
           row.names = NULL)
#>                     test all_pupils                    fiml                listwise
#> 1   t1_visual_perception   29.61462 29.615 [28.825, 30.405] 29.579 [28.458, 30.701]
#> 2               t2_cubes   24.35216 24.352 [23.821, 24.883] 24.800 [24.079, 25.521]
#> 3    t3_paper_form_board   14.22924 14.229 [13.910, 14.548] 14.303 [13.846, 14.761]
#> 4            t4_lozenges   18.00332 18.003 [16.983, 19.024] 15.966 [14.616, 17.315]
#> 5 t25_paper_form_board_r         NA 15.747 [15.272, 16.223] 15.648 [15.148, 16.149]
#> 6              t26_flags         NA 36.602 [35.334, 37.870] 36.303 [34.951, 37.656]
```

For the four tests both schools took, FIML reproduces the means of all
301 pupils (the `all_pupils` column), and listwise deletion reports the
Grant-White means. The lozenges mean is
15.97 under listwise deletion
and 18.00 under FIML. A
missing data mechanism under which the complete cases score differently from
the incomplete ones on an observed test is not MCAR, so the assumption
listwise deletion needs fails here on evidence in the data.

For the revised paper form board and the flags test, FIML moves the means a
little, by what the four tests say about how the Pasteur pupils differ. That
step is where its assumption sits. The values are missing because of the
school a pupil attended, so they are MAR given the six tests if school carries
no information about the two new tests beyond what the four old ones carry,
which no Pasteur score on the new tests can confirm or refute. School itself
cannot be added to the model to make the assumption hold: every pupil who
took the new tests attended one school, so the data say nothing about how the
new tests relate to school among pupils with the same other scores. MAR is the
weaker assumption, not a verified one, and the FIML analysis is the one that
uses everything the data hold under it.

The measurement properties of the scale, with their 95% confidence
intervals:


``` r
fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
      missing = "fiml", output = "measurement")
```



Measurement structure, per factor:

spatial: congeneric (no equality constraints)

|syntax |term          |estimate |se    |test_statistic |p_value  |ci_lower |ci_upper |
|:------|:-------------|:--------|:-----|:--------------|:--------|:--------|:--------|
|       |omega_spatial |0.761    |0.026 |28.951         |< 0.0001 |0.706    |0.808    |
|       |ave_spatial   |0.352    |0.029 |12.017         |< 0.0001 |0.297    |0.412    |
|       |H_spatial     |0.775    |0.023 |33.188         |< 0.0001 |0.726    |0.817    |

Confidence level: 95%



``` r
fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
      missing = "listwise", output = "measurement")
```



Measurement structure, per factor:

spatial: congeneric (no equality constraints)

|syntax |term          |estimate |se    |test_statistic |p_value  |ci_lower |ci_upper |
|:------|:-------------|:--------|:-----|:--------------|:--------|:--------|:--------|
|       |omega_spatial |0.773    |0.031 |25.346         |< 0.0001 |0.708    |0.828    |
|       |ave_spatial   |0.364    |0.037 |9.783          |< 0.0001 |0.295    |0.440    |
|       |H_spatial     |0.784    |0.028 |27.647         |< 0.0001 |0.724    |0.835    |

Confidence level: 95%





Omega, the reliability of the unit-weighted sum of the six tests (McDonald,
1999), is 0.761, 95% CI
[0.706, 0.808], by FIML from all
301 pupils, and 0.773
[0.708, 0.828] from the
145 Grant-White pupils. The FIML interval is
0.86 times as wide as
the listwise one. The intervals describe different populations, the two
schools together and one school, and the FIML interval is the narrower
because it also uses the 156 Pasteur pupils' scores on four of the six
tests.

### A Demonstration With a Known Answer

With planned missingness the values that are missing were never observed, so
no analysis can be checked against them. A demonstration with a known answer
deletes values that were observed. Jöreskog (1969) fitted three correlated
factors, visualization, verbal intelligence, and speed, to nine of these
tests, and all nine were given at both schools. Here paragraph comprehension
is deleted for some pupils, with a probability that is larger the lower a
pupil scored on sentence completion, a test that stays in the model: the
values are MAR given the nine tests and, by construction, not MCAR.


``` r
three <- list(
  visual = c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges"),
  verbal = c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning"),
  speed  = c("t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",
             "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals"))
nine <- unlist(three, use.names = FALSE)

set.seed(113)
mar <- holzinger_swineford[nine]
z_sentence <- as.numeric(scale(mar$t7_sentence))
p_missing <- plogis(-0.7 - 1.5 * z_sentence)
mar$t6_paragraph_comprehension[runif(nrow(mar)) < p_missing] <- NA

complete <- fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = three,
                  missing = "fiml")
listwise <- fa_confirmatory(data = mar, factors = three, missing = "listwise",
                            meanstructure = TRUE)
fiml     <- fa_confirmatory(data = mar, factors = three, missing = "fiml")

rows <- c("nu_verbal_1", "lambda_verbal_1", "phi_visual_verbal",
          "phi_verbal_speed", "omega_verbal")
data.frame(term = rows, complete = est_ci(complete, rows),
           listwise = est_ci(listwise, rows), fiml = est_ci(fiml, rows))
#>                term             complete              listwise                 fiml
#> 1       nu_verbal_1 9.183 [8.789, 9.577] 9.974 [9.503, 10.444] 9.216 [8.773, 9.659]
#> 2   lambda_verbal_1 2.969 [2.636, 3.302]  2.743 [2.339, 3.148] 2.815 [2.401, 3.228]
#> 3 phi_visual_verbal 0.459 [0.334, 0.583]  0.525 [0.377, 0.673] 0.455 [0.328, 0.582]
#> 4  phi_verbal_speed 0.283 [0.143, 0.423]  0.371 [0.212, 0.530] 0.288 [0.146, 0.429]
#> 5      omega_verbal 0.872 [0.842, 0.897]  0.873 [0.830, 0.905] 0.877 [0.847, 0.902]
```



The deletion removed 111 of the 301 paragraph comprehension
scores. The `complete` column is the analysis of the same pupils before
anything was deleted, the answer the incomplete data should recover.
Listwise deletion keeps the 190 complete pupils, among whom
pupils strong at sentence completion are more common than in the sample, and
its mean for paragraph comprehension (`nu_verbal_1`) is
9.97 against
9.18, with an interval that does not contain the complete data value; the correlation of the
verbal factor with speed moves
from 0.283 to
0.371. FIML, which keeps the sentence
completion scores of the pupils whose paragraph comprehension is missing,
gives 9.22 and
0.288, close to the complete data values on
every row. Each column is one sample, so a single row can agree or disagree
by chance. The direction of the listwise errors follows from which pupils it
keeps; FIML's consistency rests on MAR, which holds here by construction, and
on the model, which the nine tests fit only approximately (see
`vignette("sem_fit_measures")`).

### Auxiliary Variables

MAR is a statement about the variables in the analysis. When whether a value
is missing depends on a variable the model leaves out, the values can be MNAR
for the model's variables and MAR once that variable is included. Including
such variables costs little and can remove a bias that leaving them out would
leave in place (Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). Graham (2003) showed how to
include them in a FIML structural equation model without changing the model:
each auxiliary variable is a saturated correlate, correlated with every other
auxiliary and with the residual of every indicator, so it adds information to
the likelihood while the model's parameters keep their meaning and its degrees
of freedom do not change. lavaan builds that block from its `aux` argument,
which `fa_confirmatory()` passes through.

In this demonstration sentence completion goes missing more often for pupils
who scored low on word classification, a verbal test that is not in the
model.


``` r
set.seed(113)
aux_data <- holzinger_swineford[c(nine, "t8_word_classification")]
z_word <- as.numeric(scale(aux_data$t8_word_classification))
aux_data$t7_sentence[runif(nrow(aux_data)) < plogis(-0.7 - 1.5 * z_word)] <- NA

no_aux   <- fa_confirmatory(data = aux_data[nine], factors = three, missing = "fiml")
with_aux <- fa_confirmatory(data = aux_data, factors = three, missing = "fiml",
                  aux = "t8_word_classification")
#> lavaan NOTE:  
#>    auxiliary (aux) variable(s) added to the model as saturated correlates 
#>    (estimated with FIML and hidden from the output): t8_word_classification
#> Warning: lavaan->lav_object_post_check():  
#>    the covariance matrix of the residuals of the observed variables (theta) is not 
#>    positive definite; use lavInspect(fit, "theta") to investigate.

rows <- c("nu_verbal_2", "lambda_verbal_2")
data.frame(term = rows, complete = est_ci(complete, rows),
           fiml = est_ci(no_aux, rows), fiml_aux = est_ci(with_aux, rows))
#>              term                complete                    fiml
#> 1     nu_verbal_2 17.362 [16.780, 17.944] 17.875 [17.273, 18.478]
#> 2 lambda_verbal_2    4.406 [3.916, 4.897]    3.927 [3.396, 4.459]
#>                  fiml_aux
#> 1 17.423 [16.786, 18.059]
#> 2    4.115 [3.576, 4.654]
```



113 sentence completion scores were deleted. Without the
auxiliary, FIML learns about the pupils whose sentence completion is missing
only through the other two verbal tests, which do not capture all of what
word classification says about them. The sentence completion mean is
17.36 in the complete data,
17.88 by FIML without the auxiliary, and
17.42 with it, and the loading moves toward its
complete data value in the same way.

lavaan prints two things about the auxiliary fit. The note says that the
auxiliary was added as a saturated correlate and is hidden from the output.
The warning says that the covariance matrix of the residuals is not positive
definite. That matrix includes the auxiliary, whose covariances with the
verbal tests the saturated correlates specification must carry entirely
through their residuals, since the auxiliary is not allowed to correlate with
the factor. Word classification shares the verbal factor with the tests, so
those residual covariances are large relative to the residual variances of
three reliable tests, and the matrix has a negative eigenvalue
(-18.09). That is the expected signature of the
specification, not an improper solution: every residual variance is positive
(the smallest is 3.25), and the model implied covariance
matrix of the ten observed variables is positive definite (its smallest
eigenvalue is 4.13).

## What the Missing Values Cost

### The Fraction of Missing Information

The missing information principle (Orchard & Woodbury, 1972) divides the
information complete data would carry about a parameter into the information
the observed data carry and the information lost with the missing values. In
large samples the inverse of the information is the sampling variance, so for
parameter $j$ the fraction of missing information is

\[
\mathrm{FMI}_j = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{SE}^2_{C,j}}{\mathrm{SE}^2_{O,j}},
\]

where $\mathrm{SE}_{O,j}$ is the standard error of the FIML estimate and
$\mathrm{SE}_{C,j}$ the standard error it would have had if the same cases had
been observed completely (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012, Eq. 4). It is zero when
nothing is missing and approaches one as the observed data say less about the
parameter, and one minus the FMI is the asymptotic efficiency of the FIML
estimate relative to the complete data one. `fraction_missing_information()`
computes it for every free and defined parameter of a FIML fit. A percentile
bootstrap interval is opt-in; 400 replications, the fewest a 95 percent
interval is reported from (see `?dmar_bootstrap`), keep the vignette quick,
and the default is 1000.


``` r
fmi <- fraction_missing_information(fit_sp, ci_method = "percentile",
                                    B = 400, seed = 113)
fmi[fmi$op %in% c("=~", ":="), ]
```



|term                              |fmi   |fmi_ci_lower |fmi_ci_upper |width_inflation |N   |N_effective |N_target |estimate |se_observed |se_complete |
|:---------------------------------|:-----|:------------|:------------|:---------------|:---|:-----------|:--------|:--------|:-----------|:-----------|
|spatial =~ t1_visual_perception   |0.113 |0.067        |0.168        |1.061           |301 |267.136     |339.157  |4.827    |0.430       |0.405       |
|spatial =~ t2_cubes               |0.063 |0.030        |0.112        |1.033           |301 |282.009     |321.270  |2.174    |0.302       |0.292       |
|spatial =~ t3_paper_form_board    |0.075 |0.039        |0.113        |1.040           |301 |278.550     |325.259  |1.475    |0.179       |0.172       |
|spatial =~ t4_lozenges            |0.111 |0.066        |0.175        |1.061           |301 |267.508     |338.685  |5.859    |0.563       |0.530       |
|spatial =~ t25_paper_form_board_r |0.512 |0.414        |0.609        |1.431           |301 |147.001     |616.331  |1.764    |0.267       |0.186       |
|spatial =~ t26_flags              |0.506 |0.408        |0.605        |1.423           |301 |148.635     |609.555  |5.313    |0.707       |0.497       |
|loading_sum_spatial               |0.184 |0.129        |0.258        |1.107           |301 |245.688     |368.764  |21.412   |1.291       |1.166       |
|error_sum_spatial                 |0.348 |0.274        |0.423        |1.238           |301 |196.282     |461.586  |144.144  |7.733       |6.244       |
|omega_spatial                     |0.244 |0.183        |0.317        |1.150           |301 |227.492     |398.261  |0.761    |0.026       |0.022       |
|ave_spatial                       |0.221 |0.162        |0.294        |1.133           |301 |234.386     |386.546  |0.352    |0.029       |0.026       |
|H_spatial                         |0.216 |0.129        |0.388        |1.130           |301 |235.888     |384.085  |0.775    |0.023       |0.020       |

Confidence level: 95%

FMI under the unstructured information (the third estimator of Chen & Savalei, 2021), from 301 cases.

Bootstrap: 400 replications attempted, 400 returned an FMI for every parameter.

The sample FMI is imprecise unless N is several hundred (Chen & Savalei, 2021).





The loadings of the revised paper form board and the flags test have FMIs of
0.512 and 0.506, close to their missing rate of
0.518, and effective sample sizes of
147 and
149: those loadings are
estimated about as precisely as the 145 Grant-White pupils alone would
estimate them, and the Pasteur pupils add almost nothing. The loadings of the
four tests every pupil took still lose between 0.063 and
0.113 of their information, because each is estimated relative
to a factor that is measured by four tests rather than six for half the
pupils.

Omega has an FMI of 0.244, 95% CI [0.183,
0.317]: about a quarter of the sampling variance of
the reliability estimate is due to the two tests that were not given at
Pasteur.

### The Cost in Sample Size and Interval Width

A Wald interval's width is proportional to the standard error, and the
standard error to $1/\sqrt{N}$, so the FMI states the cost of the missing
values in the terms in which accuracy in parameter estimation plans a study
(Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008). Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012, pp. 488--489)
give three forms of it:

- the effective sample size, $N(1 - \mathrm{FMI})$, the number of complete
  cases that would estimate the parameter as precisely as the $N$ incomplete
  cases did;
- the target sample size, $N/(1 - \mathrm{FMI})$, the number of cases with the
  same missing data that would match the precision of $N$ complete cases; and
- the width inflation factor, $1/\sqrt{1 - \mathrm{FMI}}$, how many times
  wider the confidence interval is than complete data would have made it. An
  FMI of .56 widens it by half, and an FMI of .75 doubles it.

For omega, the 301 pupils carry the information of
227 complete cases, the same precision with the same
missing data would take 398 pupils, and the interval is
1.15 times as wide as complete data would have
made it. Because the three are monotone functions of the FMI, the limits of
its interval carry over: the effective sample size lies between
206 and
246. Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012,
p. 489) recommend reading the FMI as an effect size for the impact of the
missing values on each parameter, not against a cutoff.

### Three Estimators of the Same Fraction

Chen and Savalei (2021) compared three estimates of the observed information
behind $\mathrm{SE}_O$: the numeric Hessian of the log likelihood, which is
lavaan's default and what `lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit, fmi = TRUE)`
reports; the first term of the observed information evaluated at the model
implied moments (structured); and the same term evaluated at the unrestricted
moments (unstructured). The three are identical for a saturated model such as
a regression, and in their simulations the unstructured estimate was much less
likely to break down than the Hessian one and more precise than the
structured one (Chen & Savalei, 2021, p. 15). It is DMAR's default. It also
cannot be negative, which the other two can be.


``` r
fmi_s <- fraction_missing_information(fit_sp, information = "structured")
fmi_h <- fraction_missing_information(fit_sp, information = "hessian")
show <- function(x) formatC(ifelse(abs(x) < 5e-4, 0, x), format = "f",
                            digits = 3)
keep <- fmi$op %in% c("=~", "~1", ":=")
data.frame(term = fmi$term[keep], unstructured = show(fmi$fmi[keep]),
           structured = show(fmi_s$fmi[keep]),
           hessian = show(fmi_h$fmi[keep]))
#>                                 term unstructured structured hessian
#> 1    spatial =~ t1_visual_perception        0.113      0.111   0.128
#> 2                spatial =~ t2_cubes        0.063      0.070   0.073
#> 3     spatial =~ t3_paper_form_board        0.075      0.061   0.077
#> 4             spatial =~ t4_lozenges        0.111      0.106   0.121
#> 5  spatial =~ t25_paper_form_board_r        0.512      0.523   0.513
#> 6               spatial =~ t26_flags        0.506      0.522   0.513
#> 7            t1_visual_perception ~1        0.000     -0.003  -0.004
#> 8                        t2_cubes ~1        0.000     -0.001  -0.002
#> 9             t3_paper_form_board ~1        0.000     -0.002  -0.002
#> 10                    t4_lozenges ~1        0.000     -0.003  -0.003
#> 11         t25_paper_form_board_r ~1        0.444      0.459   0.458
#> 12                      t26_flags ~1        0.430      0.442   0.442
#> 13               loading_sum_spatial        0.184      0.217   0.201
#> 14                 error_sum_spatial        0.348      0.309   0.301
#> 15                     omega_spatial        0.244      0.263   0.246
#> 16                       ave_spatial        0.221      0.248   0.231
#> 17                         H_spatial        0.216      0.239   0.226
```



The three estimates differ by at most 0.047 on these rows. The
intercepts of the four
fully observed tests show the difference in kind: their FMI is zero, which the
unstructured estimate returns exactly and the other two miss by small negative
amounts.

### How Precise Is a Sample FMI?

A sample FMI is an estimate, and an imprecise one. In the simulations of Chen
and Savalei (2021, p. 14) it was nearly unbiased even at $N = 50$ but varied
greatly from sample to sample; with 10 to 20 percent of all values missing,
samples of several hundred gave reasonably precise estimates, and with 30
percent missing it took more than 1,000. Here
17.3
percent of the values are missing and $N$ = 301, and the interval for
omega's FMI, from 0.183 to
0.317, shows what is left of that imprecision.
Chen and Savalei list bootstrap intervals for the sample FMI as work still to
be done (p. 15), so the interval's coverage has not been studied; it shows
the sampling variability of the estimate, and its upper limit is the
conservative value to carry into a plan, as the last section does.

## The Maximum Likelihood Covariance Matrix for Exploratory Work

Exploratory factor analysis and parallel analysis start from a covariance or
correlation matrix. The complete case matrix of incomplete items is
consistent in general only under MCAR, and the pairwise matrix estimates each
covariance from a different subset of cases and need not be positive
definite. `cov_fiml()` returns the maximum likelihood estimates of the
covariance matrix and means under the multivariate normal model, the moments
of the saturated model that the EM algorithm converges to, which are
consistent under MAR given the variables included (Schafer & Graham, 2002).
Here the six spatial tests are joined by five verbal tests, all given at both
schools.


``` r
verbal <- c("t5_general_information", "t6_paragraph_comprehension",
            "t7_sentence", "t8_word_classification", "t9_word_meaning")
eleven <- c(spatial, verbal)
em <- cov_fiml(holzinger_swineford[eleven])
c(N = em$N, N_complete = em$N_complete, patterns = em$patterns)
#>          N N_complete   patterns 
#>        301        145          2
```

The matrix is the basis for exploratory decisions, the number of factors and
a first look at the loadings. Below, an exploratory factor analysis of it by
maximum likelihood, two factors rotated obliquely by direct oblimin with
$\delta = 0$ (lavaan's `"oblimin"` at its default $\gamma = 0$), is set beside
the same exploratory model fitted to the raw data twice: by two-stage
estimation (`missing = "two.stage"`, the subject of a later section), which
fits the model to the same EM moments and corrects the standard errors, and
by FIML.


``` r
efa_em <- lavaan::efa(sample.cov = em$S, sample.nobs = em$N,
                      sample.cov.rescale = FALSE, nfactors = 2,
                      rotation = "oblimin", output = "lavaan")
efa_ts <- lavaan::efa(data = holzinger_swineford[eleven], nfactors = 2,
                      rotation = "oblimin", missing = "two.stage",
                      output = "lavaan")
efa_fiml <- lavaan::efa(data = holzinger_swineford[eleven], nfactors = 2,
                        rotation = "oblimin", missing = "ml",
                        output = "lavaan")

# The spatial tests' loadings on the factor that lozenges defines.
pick <- function(s) {
  load <- s[s$op == "=~", ]
  f <- load$lhs[which.max(abs(load$est.std) *
                          (load$rhs == "t4_lozenges"))]
  load[load$lhs == f & load$rhs %in% spatial, ]
}
a   <- pick(lavaan::standardizedSolution(efa_em))
two <- pick(lavaan::standardizedSolution(efa_ts))
b   <- pick(lavaan::standardizedSolution(efa_fiml))
print(data.frame(test = a$rhs, loading_em = a$est.std, se_em = a$se,
                 loading_two_stage = two$est.std, se_two_stage = two$se,
                 loading_fiml = b$est.std, se_fiml = b$se,
                 row.names = NULL), digits = 3)
#>                     test loading_em  se_em loading_two_stage se_two_stage
#> 1   t1_visual_perception      0.659 0.0506             0.659       0.0593
#> 2               t2_cubes      0.459 0.0622             0.459       0.0681
#> 3    t3_paper_form_board      0.492 0.0602             0.492       0.0661
#> 4            t4_lozenges      0.712 0.0446             0.712       0.0510
#> 5 t25_paper_form_board_r      0.508 0.0591             0.508       0.0918
#> 6              t26_flags      0.634 0.0520             0.634       0.0801
#>   loading_fiml se_fiml
#> 1        0.647  0.0582
#> 2        0.460  0.0651
#> 3        0.490  0.0645
#> 4        0.715  0.0499
#> 5        0.555  0.0912
#> 6        0.591  0.0874
```



The EM matrix and the two-stage fit give the same loadings, since both fit the model
to the same moments, and the FIML loadings are similar without being
identical, as a full information estimate need not equal a two-stage one. The
matrix gives the exploratory decisions what they need. The standard errors
are another matter. A program given `S` and `N` treats them as complete data
on `N` cases, and the EM matrix of 301 incomplete cases carries less
information than that. The two-stage standard errors of the loadings of the
revised paper form board and the flags test are
1.55 and 1.54 times the ones the EM
matrix gave, and the FIML standard errors
1.54 and 1.68 times, of the
order of the width inflation factors their FMIs implied in the confirmatory
model, 1.43
and 1.42. `em$N` counts the
cases used; it is not an effective sample size (Enders & Peugh, 2004;
Savalei & Bentler, 2009). Intervals, tests, and fit statistics for an
exploratory solution come from a two-stage or a FIML fit. A parallel analysis
that compares the eigenvalues of the EM matrix with those of random data
faces the same choice of $N$ for the random data, and `em$N` does not express the parameter-specific
information behind the matrix.

This demonstration calls lavaan's EFA interface directly. DMAR's
`fa_exploratory()`
provides a common parameter table, confidence intervals, and explicit method
metadata for its documented continuous and ordered analysis routes.

### When an Unrestricted Estimate Is Unavailable

An EM algorithm can converge to an interior stationary point even when the
unrestricted normal likelihood has no finite global maximum. A complete-case
count by itself is also insufficient. DMAR examines candidate variable sets
and every row observing each set. A full-support affine collapse gives a
sufficient unbounded-likelihood diagnosis; an overdetermined relation at
numerical precision is reported separately as instability. A capped,
near-singular iterate without such a certificate is a fitting failure,
not proof of nonexistence. Failure to find one of these obstacles does not
certify existence or uniqueness.

This distinction changes what can be reported. Analytic alpha, an
observed-denominator omega, FMI, and two-stage estimation need unrestricted moments.
An otherwise proper, identified constrained FIML factor model can still
supply its own estimates and H0-based uncertainty. In that case DMAR
withholds H1-based fit indices and residual correlations and retains the
qualification in the printed and exported results. A linked planned-missing
form design can have the same distinction: factor structure can identify a
relation whose unrestricted covariance no case observes.

An incomplete-data correlation matrix used for parallel analysis does not
come with one universal effective sample size. `parallel_analysis()` labels
its reference size as a benchmark and distinguishes Monte Carlo uncertainty
in null quantiles from sampling uncertainty in observed eigenvalues. Direct
`fa_exploratory()` with FIML preserves the raw-data likelihood and its corresponding
parameter uncertainty instead of treating estimated moments as complete data.

## Small Samples: A *t* Reference Distribution

### Maximum Likelihood

A Wald interval is the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times its
standard error. The normal quantile treats the standard error as known,
which it is only in the limit, and with few cases, or few effective cases
once the missing information is subtracted, the interval is too short. Von
Hippel (2016) kept the maximum likelihood estimate and its standard error and
referred their ratio to a *t* distribution on degrees of freedom that shrink
with the fraction of missing information; for a regression coefficient,

\[
\nu_j = \max\{3,\; N(1 - \mathrm{FMI}_j) - k\},
\]

the complete data degrees of freedom $N - k$ (with $k$ the slopes and the
intercept) with $N$ replaced by the coefficient's effective sample size, and
bounded below at 3. In his simulations of bivariate normal data with half of
one variable missing, the normal FIML intervals for a regression's intercept
and slope covered 5 to 6 points below the nominal 95 percent at $n = 25$, and
the *t* intervals brought the coverage of most parameters to within 2 points
of nominal (as summarized on the help page of `df_missing()`).

A pilot of 50 pupils drawn at random from both schools shows the rule at
work. Visual perception is regressed on lozenges and on the flags test, which
only the Grant-White pupils in the pilot took. `mlmr()` fits the regression
by FIML, and `wald_df = "missing_information"` applies von Hippel's rule to
each coefficient.


``` r
set.seed(113)
pilot <- holzinger_swineford[sample.int(nrow(holzinger_swineford), 50),
                             c("t1_visual_perception", "t4_lozenges",
                               "t26_flags")]
colSums(is.na(pilot))
#> t1_visual_perception          t4_lozenges            t26_flags 
#>                    0                    0                   28

fit_z <- mlmr(t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges + t26_flags, data = pilot,
              ci_method = "wald", effect_sizes = FALSE)
fit_t <- mlmr(t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges + t26_flags, data = pilot,
              ci_method = "wald", effect_sizes = FALSE,
              wald_df = "missing_information")
summary(fit_t)
#> 
#> Call:
#> mlmr(formula = t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges + t26_flags, 
#>     data = pilot, ci_method = "wald", effect_sizes = FALSE, wald_df = "missing_information")
#> 
#> Missing data: fiml | Estimator: ML | SE: standard
#> Sample size (used by lavaan): 50   Complete cases: 22
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  
#> (Intercept)  16.7998     6.5899   2.549   0.0215 *
#> t4_lozenges   0.1439     0.1998   0.720   0.4784  
#> t26_flags     0.2807     0.2566   1.094   0.2924  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> Wald intervals and p-values: t reference on von Hippel's (2016) missing
#> information degrees of freedom, max(3, N(1 - FMI) - k), with N = 50 and k = 3:
#>    term        fmi   df   
#>    (Intercept) 0.622 15.90
#>    t4_lozenges 0.471 23.45
#>    t26_flags   0.659 14.05
#> 
#> Confidence intervals (method: wald, level = 0.95):
#>               2.5 %  97.5 %
#> (Intercept)  2.8230 30.7766
#> t4_lozenges -0.2690  0.5569
#> t26_flags   -0.2695  0.8309
#> 
#> Residual std. error (ML): 5.635 on 19 residual degrees of freedom
#> Model implied R-squared: 0.2596,   Adjusted R-squared: 0.1817,   Cohen's f^2: 0.3507
#> Log likelihood: -404.2   AIC: 826.4   BIC: 843.6
```



Only 22 of the 50 pupils in the pilot took the flags test. The
fractions of missing information under the coefficient table are high, and
the degrees of freedom are low: 14.0 for the flags slope
and 23.5 for the lozenges slope, against the
47 that complete data would give. The *t* intervals are wider than the
normal ones by factors of 1.09 and
1.05. The
degrees of freedom are what `df_missing()` returns from the fraction of
missing information table, and its second rule, von Hippel's general one,
needs the complete data degrees of freedom instead:


``` r
fmi_pilot <- fraction_missing_information(fit_z)
slopes <- fmi_pilot[fmi_pilot$op == "~", ]
df_missing(slopes, k = 3)
```



|term                               |df     |df_unbounded |fmi   |N  |k  |df_complete |at_floor |
|:----------------------------------|:------|:------------|:-----|:--|:--|:-----------|:--------|
|t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges |23.452 |23.452       |0.471 |50 |3  |NA          |FALSE    |
|t1_visual_perception ~ t26_flags   |14.048 |14.048       |0.659 |50 |3  |NA          |FALSE    |

Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule,
N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3



``` r
df_missing(slopes, df_complete = 50 - 3, method = "complete_df")
```



|term                               |df     |df_unbounded |fmi   |N  |k  |df_complete |at_floor |
|:----------------------------------|:------|:------------|:-----|:--|:--|:-----------|:--------|
|t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges |23.870 |23.870       |0.471 |50 |NA |47          |FALSE    |
|t1_visual_perception ~ t26_flags   |15.384 |15.384       |0.659 |50 |NA |47          |FALSE    |

Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 32) complete data rule,
df_complete (1 - fmi) (df_complete + 1) / (df_complete + 3), bounded below at 3



Two cautions belong beside these numbers. The *t* distribution is an
approximation, since the small-sample distribution of a FIML estimate is not
exactly *t*. And with an FMI estimated from 50 cases, the degrees of freedom
inherit the imprecision of the FMI described above.

The numerical calibration figures below are conditional on the samples the
study kept, which it selected with an H1 eligibility rule that is less strict
than DMAR's affine-collapse diagnostic. That diagnostic can remove many more
samples, especially in the smallest studies with many incomplete items, and
the study did not establish coverage among the samples that diagnostic keeps. Replaying
observed-data eligibility alone does not validate DMAR's FMI refits or
information diagnostics. The degrees-of-freedom keyword is an approximate,
opt-in rule, not a coverage guarantee. Alpha's FMI keyword is refused; a small
selected pool with apparently favorable coverage would not justify enabling it.

Von Hippel's evidence covers regression coefficients and moments. For factor
loadings and omega, DMAR's own calibration study (one factor models fit by
FIML, $N$ from 30 to 200, normal data fit by ML and nonnormal data by MLR,
2000 replications in each of 60 conditions) found that the same rule with
$k = 1$, $\max\{3,\; N(1 - \mathrm{FMI}) - 1\}$, brought the coverage of
the loadings and of omega closer to 95 percent than the normal reference did
(a mean distance of .017 and .018 from .95 in the small samples with missing
values, against .025 and .024). Averaged over a condition's loadings, the
coverage was at most 95.02 percent and omega's at most 95.5; with missing
values no single loading's was above 96 (the highest was 95.95), and without
them, where the rule is $t$ on $N - 1$, one reached 96.3, where the normal
reference reached 96.2. So `fa_confirmatory()` accepts
`wald_df = "missing_information"` for its loadings, whose other rows keep the
normal reference (its omega, AVE, and *H* take limits formed on the logit
scale, where the same rule overcovered omega, at up to 96.45 percent), and
`reliability_omega()` accepts it for the model implied coefficient's `"ml"`
and `"mlr"` intervals. For alpha the
normal FIML interval was already close to nominal, the *t* reference came
barely closer on average, and in one condition it covered 96.6 percent,
above the 96 percent the study's decision rule allowed, so no rule passed
(that condition is the one where the study's fit of alpha's saturated model
converged in only half the replications, and without it the rule would have
passed; the rule was fixed before the run).
`reliability_alpha()` therefore takes a number through `wald_df`, the
analyst's choice, as a check on how much a plausible number of degrees of
freedom would widen its interval.

### Multiple Imputation

Multiple imputation fills each missing value with draws from its predictive
distribution, analyzes each completed data set, and pools the results by
Rubin's (1987) rules. With $m$ imputations, the within-imputation variance
$\bar U$ (the mean squared standard error), and the between-imputation
variance $B$ (the variance of the $m$ estimates), the total variance is
$T = \bar U + (1 + 1/m)B$, and the share of it due to the missing values is
the imputation estimate of the FMI. Barnard and Rubin (1999) gave degrees of
freedom for the pooled *t* interval that do not exceed the complete data
degrees of freedom, which Rubin's large-sample formula can. DMAR does not
impute; `df_barnard_rubin()` pools what an imputation package produced. Here
mice imputes the flags test by the normal linear model (`method = "norm"`),
the model FIML assumes, 20 times.


``` r
imp <- mice::mice(pilot, m = 20, method = "norm", seed = 113,
                  printFlag = FALSE)
fits <- lapply(seq_len(20), function(j)
  lm(t1_visual_perception ~ t4_lozenges + t26_flags,
     data = mice::complete(imp, j)))
est <- t(sapply(fits, coef))
u   <- t(sapply(fits, function(f) diag(vcov(f))))
br  <- df_barnard_rubin(between = apply(est, 2, var), within = colMeans(u),
                        m = 20, df_complete = 50 - 3)
br
```



|term        |df     |df_unbounded |gamma |relative_increase |total_variance |nu_m   |nu_obs |at_floor |
|:-----------|:------|:------------|:-----|:-----------------|:--------------|:------|:------|:--------|
|(Intercept) |9.053  |9.053        |0.731 |2.716             |54.808         |35.570 |12.143 |FALSE    |
|t4_lozenges |12.651 |12.651       |0.622 |1.647             |0.059          |49.074 |17.045 |FALSE    |
|t26_flags   |7.935  |7.935        |0.767 |3.289             |0.087          |32.309 |10.519 |FALSE    |

Degrees of freedom: Barnard and Rubin's (1999) rule for m = 20 imputations,
1 / (1 / nu_m + 1 / nu_obs) with df_complete = 47, bounded below at 3



``` r

pooled <- colMeans(est)
crit <- qt(0.975, br$df)
data.frame(term = names(pooled),
           mi = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", pooled,
                        pooled - crit * sqrt(br$total_variance),
                        pooled + crit * sqrt(br$total_variance)),
           fiml = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", coef(fit_t), fit_t$ci[, 1],
                          fit_t$ci[, 2]))
#>          term                     mi                   fiml
#> 1 (Intercept) 18.948 [2.215, 35.680] 16.800 [2.823, 30.777]
#> 2 t4_lozenges  0.232 [-0.295, 0.758]  0.144 [-0.269, 0.557]
#> 3   t26_flags  0.186 [-0.494, 0.865]  0.281 [-0.270, 0.831]
```



The imputations' estimates of the FMI (`gamma`) are higher than FIML's for every coefficient
(0.767 against
0.659 for the flags slope), and
the multiple imputation intervals are 1.20 to
1.27 times as wide as FIML's. Under the same normal model
the two approaches estimate the same quantities, and they agree in large
samples as the number of imputations grows; von Hippel's general rule
(`method = "complete_df"` above) is the limit of Barnard and Rubin's degrees
of freedom as it does. In a sample of 50 they need not agree: the
between-imputation variance is estimated from 20 values, and the imputation
model's parameters are drawn from their posterior on every imputation. Von
Hippel (2016) compared the two in samples of 25 and 100, and his title states
what he found, that maximum likelihood can beat multiple imputation in small
samples. `floor = 0` reproduces Barnard and Rubin's formula, and with it the
degrees of freedom that `pool()` in mice reports.

## Two-Stage Maximum Likelihood

A third consistent estimator under MAR fits the model in two stages (Yuan &
Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009). The first stage estimates the means
and covariances by maximum likelihood under the saturated model, the EM
moments of `cov_fiml()`, from every case and any auxiliary variables. The
second fits the model to those moments as if they were complete data. The
estimates are consistent under MAR and only marginally less efficient than
FIML's (Savalei & Bentler, 2009), and auxiliary variables enter the first
stage alone, which is simpler than the saturated correlates of FIML. What the
second stage cannot give alone is a standard error or a test: it treats the EM
moments as complete data, so its naive standard errors are too small and its
naive chi square does not have a chi square distribution. `fa_confirmatory()` with
`missing = "two_stage"` reports the two-stage sandwich standard errors and the
residual based statistic of Savalei and Bentler (2009), which is
asymptotically chi square and in their simulations outperformed the FIML
likelihood ratio statistic.


``` r
fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
      missing = "two_stage", output = "measurement")
```



Measurement structure, per factor:

spatial: congeneric (no equality constraints)

|syntax |term          |estimate |se    |test_statistic |p_value  |ci_lower |ci_upper |
|:------|:-------------|:--------|:-----|:--------------|:--------|:--------|:--------|
|       |omega_spatial |0.763    |0.026 |29.815         |< 0.0001 |0.709    |0.809    |
|       |ave_spatial   |0.354    |0.029 |12.216         |< 0.0001 |0.299    |0.413    |
|       |H_spatial     |0.778    |0.023 |33.939         |< 0.0001 |0.729    |0.819    |

Confidence level: 95%

Two-stage maximum likelihood: the model fit to the EM estimates of the means and covariances, with normal theory standard errors (Savalei & Bentler, 2009)





Omega is 0.763 [0.709,
0.809], against 0.761
[0.706, 0.808] by FIML. The fit of
the model is where the two-stage approach earns its place. Zhang and Savalei
(2023) showed that the RMSEA and CFI computed after FIML in the usual way do
not estimate the values complete data would give, proposed corrected
versions for FIML (FIML-C) and for two-stage estimation (TS), and found that
both estimated the complete data values with little bias, while the usual
FIML indices often performed poorly. Of their two-stage versions they
recommend TS V2, whose correction rests on the sandwich of the observed and
first order information of the saturated model, an estimate of the sampling
covariance matrix of the EM moments that does not assume normality.
`sem_fit_measures()` reports the corrected indices by default for both fits.
With `missing = "two_stage"`, whose standard errors and residual based
statistic are normal theory ones, the two-stage indices are the normal
theory analog of TS V2, which puts the inverse of the observed information
in place of the sandwich and which Zhang and Savalei did not study;
`missing = "robust_two_stage"` gives TS V2 itself. The usual FIML indices
are reported on request, and the usual two-stage ones are refused, since the
naive statistic they rest on is not chi square distributed:


``` r
fit_ts <- fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = spatial_factor,
                missing = "two_stage", output = "fit")
fm_fiml  <- sem_fit_measures(fit_sp)
fm_naive <- sem_fit_measures(fit_sp, version = "standard")
fm_ts    <- sem_fit_measures(fit_ts)
fm_ts
```

Confidence level: 90%

Version: robust (auto: the fit uses two-stage estimation (missing = "two.stage"))

Chi square: two-stage residual based statistic (Savalei & Bentler, 2009); robust measures: two-stage corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), the normal theory analog of TS V2

Sample size: N = 301 in 1 group; multiplier a = 301 (lavaan's normal likelihood forms T with N)



``` r

fit_row <- function(fm) {
  vv <- function(t) fm$value[match(t, fm$term)]
  c(chi_square = sprintf("%.2f", vv("chi_square")),
    p = format_p(vv("p_chi_square")),
    rmsea_90 = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", vv("rmsea"),
                       vv("rmsea_ci_lower"), vv("rmsea_ci_upper")),
    cfi = sprintf("%.3f", vv("cfi")))
}
noquote(rbind(fiml_usual = fit_row(fm_naive),
              fiml_corrected = fit_row(fm_fiml),
              two_stage = fit_row(fm_ts)))
#>                chi_square p      rmsea_90             cfi  
#> fiml_usual     11.98      0.2143 0.033 [0.000, 0.077] 0.988
#> fiml_corrected 11.98      0.2143 0.066 [0.000, 0.123] 0.968
#> two_stage      10.85      0.2860 0.064 [0.000, 0.119] 0.969
```



The usual FIML RMSEA, 0.033, understates the misfit
that the corrected value, 0.066, estimates, and the
usual CFI of 0.988 overstates the fit relative to the
corrected 0.968; the two-stage indices are close to the
corrected FIML ones. Treating the EM moments as complete data would have given a chi
square of 27.91 on 9 degrees of freedom,
$p$ = 0.0010,
a rejection of the model; the residual based statistic is
10.85, $p$ = 0.2860. The RMSEA
intervals are at 90 percent, the conventional level and DMAR's default for
every RMSEA interval, whose limits are then the two one-sided tests at .05
(see `vignette("sem_fit_measures")`); `conf_level = 0.95` gives 95 percent
intervals. Zhang and
Savalei advise against mixing the two: an analysis estimated by FIML reports
the FIML corrected indices, and two-stage indices belong with two-stage
estimates.

## Reliability Under Missing Data

### Omega and Alpha by FIML

`reliability_omega()` and `reliability_alpha()`, like `fa_confirmatory()`,
fit incomplete items by FIML by default (`missing = "fiml"`), and they take
`"two_stage"` and `aux` as well, so the reliability of a scale with incomplete
items comes from every case; the calls below name the method, and
`missing = "listwise"` asks for the complete cases alone. Robust omega, the
default denominator, divides the variance the single factor accounts for by
the composite variance estimated from the data (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit,
2016); its interval is a bootstrap, here with 400 replications, the fewest
a 95 percent percentile interval is reported from, where a reported analysis
deserves the default 10000.


``` r
om_fiml <- reliability_omega(data = holzinger_swineford[spatial],
                             missing = "fiml", ci_method = "percentile",
                             B = 400, seed = 113)
om_fiml
```



|term       |value |
|:----------|:-----|
|estimate   |0.753 |
|se         |0.031 |
|ci_lower   |0.688 |
|ci_upper   |0.814 |
|conf_level |0.950 |
|N          |301   |
|N_complete |145   |
|n_items    |6     |

Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)

Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.111 (t3_paper_form_board with t25_paper_form_board_r)

Bootstrap: 400 replications attempted, 400 returned a value



``` r
om_lw <- reliability_omega(data = holzinger_swineford[spatial],
                           missing = "listwise", ci_method = "percentile",
                           B = 400, seed = 113)
al_fiml <- reliability_alpha(data = holzinger_swineford[spatial],
                             missing = "fiml")
al_fiml
```



|term       |value |
|:----------|:-----|
|estimate   |0.725 |
|se         |0.023 |
|ci_lower   |0.679 |
|ci_upper   |0.771 |
|conf_level |0.950 |
|N          |301   |
|N_complete |145   |
|n_items    |6     |





Robust omega is 0.753, 95% CI
[0.688, 0.814],
from all 301 pupils, against
0.772 [0.697,
0.830] from the 145 complete
cases. The table reports both `N` and `N_complete`, so the cost of listwise
deletion is in view. Alpha by FIML is the classical coefficient computed from
the FIML (EM) covariance matrix, 0.725
[0.679, 0.771]; it
assumes equal loadings, which these six tests do not have, and is reported
here only beside omega.

### Ordered Items: Pairwise Deletion and Multiple Imputation

Categorical omega (Green & Yang, 2009) is the reliability of a sum of ordered
categories. Its single-factor model is fitted to polychoric correlations by
weighted least squares, which has no full information form here, so
`reliability_omega_categorical()` offers two other treatments of incomplete
rows besides listwise deletion. Pairwise deletion estimates each threshold and
polychoric correlation from the rows that observe its items. It uses more of
the data than listwise deletion, not a weaker assumption: without covariates
in the model it is consistent only under MCAR (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010), and
under MAR Shi, Lee, Fairchild, and Maydeu-Olivares (2020) found its estimates
severely biased. Multiple imputation is consistent under MAR given the items
and any auxiliary variables. Its interval is bootstrap then impute (Schomaker
& Heumann, 2018): each bootstrap sample of the incomplete rows is imputed
several times, and the percentile interval of the replicate means is the
confidence interval.

The Holzinger and Swineford tests are scored as counts of correct answers,
not as ordered categories, so for this section each test is cut at its
quartiles into four ordered categories, as a four-point rating would record
it.


``` r
cat4 <- as.data.frame(lapply(holzinger_swineford[spatial], function(x) {
  cuts <- stats::quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  findInterval(x, cuts, left.open = TRUE) + 1L
}))

oc_lw <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = cat4,
                                       ci_method = "percentile",
                                       B = 400, seed = 113)
oc_pw <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = cat4, missing = "pairwise",
                                       ci_method = "percentile",
                                       B = 400, seed = 113)
oc_pw
```



|term       |value |
|:----------|:-----|
|estimate   |0.708 |
|se         |0.035 |
|ci_lower   |0.633 |
|ci_upper   |0.774 |
|conf_level |0.950 |
|N          |301   |
|N_complete |145   |
|n_items    |6     |

Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the unrestricted polychoric correlations (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016)

Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.143 (t25_paper_form_board_r with t26_flags)

Bootstrap: 400 replications attempted, 400 returned a value

Missing data: pairwise deletion, consistent only when values are missing completely at random, as listwise deletion is (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010); it uses more of the data, not a weaker assumption, and missing = "mi" is the remedy when values are missing at random



``` r
# B = 400 is the fewest replications a 95 percent percentile interval is
# reported from and keeps the vignette quick; under imputation the default
# is 1000.
# ncpus = 2 spreads the replications over two processes, and a seed gives
# the same result whatever ncpus is.
oc_mi <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = cat4, missing = "mi",
                                       ci_method = "percentile",
                                       B = 400, seed = 113, ncpus = 2)
oc_mi
```



|term       |value |
|:----------|:-----|
|estimate   |0.715 |
|se         |0.035 |
|ci_lower   |0.640 |
|ci_upper   |0.783 |
|conf_level |0.950 |
|N          |301   |
|N_complete |145   |
|n_items    |6     |

Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the unrestricted polychoric correlations (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016)

Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.156 (t25_paper_form_board_r with t26_flags)

Bootstrap: 400 replications attempted, 400 returned a value

Missing data: multiple imputation by predictive mean matching (mice), assuming values missing at random given the items; interval by bootstrap then impute (Schomaker & Heumann, 2018)

Imputations: 20 of the observed data (von Hippel's rule asks for 18, the floor is 20); 20 in each bootstrap replication; fraction of missing information 0.25 (95% upper limit 0.28); imputation noise widens the interval by about 0.613%





Listwise deletion gives 0.725 [0.641, 0.799] from the 145
Grant-White pupils, pairwise deletion 0.708 [0.633, 0.774], and multiple
imputation 0.715 [0.640, 0.783] from all 301. Pairwise deletion
estimates the thresholds of the two new tests and their correlations with the
old ones from the Grant-White pupils, and the other correlations from both
schools, which mixes two populations unless the values are MCAR, and the
lozenges means showed that they are not. Imputation fills in the Pasteur
pupils' categories on the new tests from their categories on the old ones, the
same MAR assumption FIML made above. The three estimates are close in these
data, which is a property of these data and not something to expect; the
lines under the imputation table say how many imputations the point estimate
averaged, the FMI the replications estimated for the coefficient, and how
much the imputation noise widened the interval.

## Factor Scores Under Missing Data

Under FIML each case is scored from the items it answered, so the precision
of a factor score depends on the case's missing data pattern.
`factor_scores()` returns both standard scores, the regression score and the
Bartlett score, with a standard error and an interval for every case, and the
determinacy of each score, its correlation with the factor, for each pattern.


``` r
scores <- factor_scores(fit_sp, data = holzinger_swineford)
scores
```



Factor scores: regression and Bartlett scores, 1 factor (spatial), 301 rows

Fit: ML, missing = "ml"; scored from the fit

|row |factor  |regression |se    |95% CI          |Bartlett |se    |95% CI           |
|:---|:-------|:----------|:-----|:---------------|:--------|:-----|:----------------|
|1   |spatial |-1.038     |0.552 |[-2.120, 0.044] |-1.493   |0.662 |[-2.790, -0.196] |
|2   |spatial |-0.201     |0.552 |[-1.283, 0.881] |-0.289   |0.662 |[-1.586, 1.008]  |
|3   |spatial |-0.564     |0.552 |[-1.645, 0.518] |-0.811   |0.662 |[-2.108, 0.487]  |

(the first 3 rows of each factor)

Determinacy, the correlation of each score with its factor, by missing data pattern; min_r, the lowest correlation two sets of scores equally consistent with the model can have (2 x the regression score's determinacy squared, minus 1; Guttman, 1955):

```
 pattern   n  factor items regression Bartlett min_r
       1 145 spatial   6/6      0.880    0.880 0.550
       2 156 spatial   4/6      0.834    0.834 0.391
```

Intervals treat the fitted parameters as known: regression intervals
are posterior (empirical Bayes) intervals, Bartlett intervals Wald
intervals for each case's factor value. In a later regression, use
regression scores for a predictor and Bartlett scores for an outcome,
each from its own measurement model (Skrondal & Laake, 2001); for
relations among factors, one-step SEM or structural after measurement
(lavaan::sam()) is preferred to any regression among scores.

Confidence level: 95%





A Grant-White pupil, scored from six tests, has a score whose determinacy is
0.880; a Pasteur pupil, scored from four, 0.834, with a
standard error of the regression score of 0.552 against
0.474. For one factor the square of the determinacy is
coefficient *H* (Hancock & Mueller, 2001), the reliability of the optimally
weighted composite: 0.775 for the complete pattern, the `H_spatial`
of the FIML fit, 0.775. A regression score computed this way, from each case's own
observed items with the model's estimates, is what Estabrook and Neale (2013)
call the full maximum likelihood score (as the help page of `factor_scores()`
explains), and in their simulation it was more reliable under missing data
than sum scores. The lines under
the table say which score belongs where in a later analysis; for relations
among factors, a latent variable model estimates them without the bias a
regression among scores carries.

## Planning the Next Study

A reliability coefficient that will be estimated from incomplete data needs a
larger sample for the same interval width. `ss_aipe_reliability()` takes the
anticipated FMI of the coefficient through `fmi` and divides the complete data
$N - 1$ by $1 - \mathrm{FMI}$. The planning FMI is not the proportion of
missing values. It comes from a pilot study or a comparable data set analyzed
the way the planned study will be, here the FMI of omega estimated above,
and because a sample FMI is imprecise, the upper limit of its interval is the
conservative choice. Suppose the next study gives the same six tests with the
same planned missingness and wants a 95 percent interval for omega no wider
than .10, with the loadings and error variances of the FIML fit as the
planning values. They are taken on the scale of the test scores, as the fit
estimated them: the planner plans for the coefficient of the scores as they
are, the omega estimated above.


``` r
# The unstandardized loadings and error variances of the FIML fit.
lambda <- tab_sp$estimate[match(paste0("lambda_spatial_", 1:6), tab_sp$term)]
psi <- tab_sp$estimate[match(paste0("psi_spatial_", 1:6), tab_sp$term)]
fmi_omega <- fmi[fmi$term == "omega_spatial", ]

plan_complete <- ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Congeneric",
                                     type = "Factor Analytic", width = 0.10,
                                     n_items = 6, true_factor_loading = lambda,
                                     true_residual_var = psi)
plan_missing <- ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Congeneric",
                                    type = "Factor Analytic", width = 0.10,
                                    n_items = 6, true_factor_loading = lambda,
                                    true_residual_var = psi,
                                    fmi = fmi_omega$fmi_ci_upper)
plan_missing
```



|term        |value |
|:-----------|:-----|
|necessary_N |341   |

Confidence level: 95%

Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.317 for the coefficient; with complete data, N = 233.





Complete data would need 233 cases. Planned with the upper
limit of the FMI interval, 0.317, the study needs
341; planned with the point estimate,
0.244, it would need 308.

The standardized loadings of the same fit would be the wrong planning values
here. They describe omega of standardized tests, which is nearly the same
number (0.762 against 0.761) but not the same
coefficient: the six tests' variances run from about
8 to 82, and the sampling variance
of omega depends on them. Planned from the standardized loadings, the
complete data study would get 209 cases, about
10 percent too few for the
coefficient estimated above.

`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()` checks such a plan by simulation. It
simulates parallel items with each item score missing completely at random
with probability `missing_prop`, analyzes every replication by FIML, and
reports the realized interval widths together with the FMI the simulated
missing data actually cost the coefficient. The check below simulates six
parallel items whose reliability is the omega estimated above, with a
`missing_prop` chosen so that the simulated data lose about the planned share
of information. Every replication fits a model, so 100 replications keep the
vignette quick where a reported check deserves 1000.


``` r
omega_hat <- m_fiml$estimate[m_fiml$term == "omega_spatial"]
set.seed(113)
check <- ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(
  true_reliability = omega_hat, supposed_reliability = omega_hat,
  n_items = 6, width = 0.10, estimator = "omega",
  fmi = fmi_omega$fmi_ci_upper, missing_prop = 0.35, G = 100)
check
```



|term                 |value |
|:--------------------|:-----|
|mean_reliability     |0.763 |
|median_reliability   |0.761 |
|sd_reliability       |0.022 |
|mean_ci_width        |0.099 |
|median_ci_width      |0.100 |
|sd_ci_width          |0.010 |
|pct_ci_less_width    |0.510 |
|pct_ci_miss_low      |0.060 |
|pct_ci_miss_high     |0.000 |
|total_type_I_error   |0.060 |
|total_N              |310   |
|n_items              |6     |
|true_reliability     |0.761 |
|supposed_reliability |0.761 |
|width                |0.100 |
|conf_level           |0.950 |

Replications: 100

Confidence level: 95%

Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.317; simulated with each item score missing completely at random with probability 0.35 and analyzed by full information maximum likelihood.
The fraction of missing information the simulated data realized for the coefficient averaged 0.317 over the 100 replications in which it was computed.





The plan for parallel items called for 310 cases. The simulated
data realized a mean FMI of 0.317 for omega
against the 0.317 planned, and the intervals averaged
0.099 wide against the .10 planned. When the realized
FMI is close to the planned one and the mean width near the target, the plan
carries the missing data it was made for. The mechanism simulated here is
MCAR spread over all six items, not the planned missingness of two tests, so
the check speaks to the adjustment, not to this design's FMI; that comes from
the pilot, and the mean realized FMI of a simulation that mimics the planned
study is a planning value that does not suffer from the imprecision of one
sample.

## What to Report

An analysis of incomplete data reports what was missing, how it was
handled, under what assumption, and what it cost. For the spatial tests:

> The revised paper form board and flags tests were given only at the
> Grant-White school, so 156 of 301 pupils
> (51.8 percent) have no score on either. The
> single-factor model was fitted by full information maximum likelihood,
> which assumes that the scores are missing at random given the six tests;
> listwise deletion would have analyzed one school only, whose lozenges mean
> differed from the other's by
> 3.93
> points. Coefficient omega was 0.761, 95% CI
> [0.706, 0.808]. The fraction of
> missing information for omega was 0.244, 95% CI
> [0.183, 0.317]: the
> 301 pupils carried the information of about
> 227 complete cases, and the interval is
> 1.15 times as wide as complete data would have
> made it.
